verdict: ENRICH, but through the Tier 1 sources, not through the essay. Do NOT cite Tonon as support anywhere and do NOT create a research page for the deposit. Nature of the deposit: Zenodo resource type 'Working paper' (not peer-reviewed), but the text is an MSc-course-style essay ('This essay ...', Part A/Part B structure, 10 pp including references) by a current Oxford continuing-education master's student with no publication record. Under EDITORIAL 4c that is Tier 2 at best (and not a practitioner or advocate of note); claims resting only on it are D-grade. If T1 wants to credit it at all, a Sources-only line as the pointer from which the Tier 1 sources were found is the maximum, phrased impersonally; the reader-facing prose should not mention it. Dedup: 10.5281/zenodo.23002574 is the Zenodo CONCEPT DOI that resolves to this same record (record id 23002575, version 3 per revision field, created 2026-09-27); it is not a separate earlier deposit. claim_grade: Essay as a source: D, Tier 2 at best (unaffiliated-with-publication-record MSc student; non-peer-reviewed Zenodo working paper). Figures reached through Tier 1 sources: Peterson 2009 JLE estimates A for what the report says (World Bank, official body), with the scope caveat; Sandroni 2011 and Friendly 2017 B (Lincoln Institute publication by a former Sao Paulo planning director who is an FGV economics professor; academic IMFG paper by a PhD planner, Assistant Professor at Utrecht); Mahendra et al. 2020 B (WRI working paper, Tier 1 institution); Gibson 2025 A for statute dates (Cambridge Dept of Land Economy). Essay claims whose Tier 1 source was not reached (Amigo-attributed figures, McAllister p.124, Crook & Whitehead p.375, Nobre post-2008 OODC halving, Christophers 10% landmass, Oxley/Whitehead 40%/20% affordable-housing split) stay D/unverified.
content_summary: ARGUMENT (Tonon pp.1-2, 5, 7): LVC is widely recommended but under-deployed; the constraints are institutional/political rather than technical, so they need better governance rather than better instruments; three mutually reinforcing clusters (technical, legal, market); LVC works only where standardised design, legal durability, participatory governance and redistributive intent coexist (p.2, p.7); concludes publicly created land value should be treated as a public asset, not a private entitlement (p.1, p.7). Leans on Fainstein's (2010) equity/democracy/diversity test, Christophers (2018) and Wolf-Powers (2024) (a Georgist-legacy article in Environment and Planning A) for the framing. ENGLAND, as the essay states it, with what the Tier 1 check found: (a) Viability assessment (Tonon p.3): negotiated s106 viability models are 'acutely sensitive to minor input changes' and developers control the inputs (attributed to McAllister 2017 p.124, not read); developer contributions in London 2005-2017 varied with negotiating capacity rather than land-value uplift (McAllister, Shepherd & Wyatt 2018, not read). Essay's remedy (p.5-6): publish non-negotiable official land values; Calavita & Mallach 2009 (Land Lines) said to find formulaic obligations outperform negotiated ones. (b) JLE (Tonon p.3): completed 1999, GBP3.5bn public cost. Three studies: one found land-value impacts impossible to estimate (Atisreal & Geofutures 2005 for TfL); one put Canary Wharf uplift at GBP300m to GBP2.7bn (Jones Lang LaSalle 2004 for TfL); one put it at GBP40m (Mitchell & Vickers 2003, Lincoln Institute). The essay calls this a '67-fold discrepancy' (2.7bn/40m) and cites Peterson 2009. VERIFIED against Peterson 2009, printed pp.37-38 (PDF pp.56-57): the three studies and numbers are exactly as stated; Peterson draws the conclusion that parcel-by-parcel betterment is impractical for major rail and that Crossrail was instead financed by negotiated 'voluntary' contributions, with Canary Wharf developers and BAA reportedly contributing a combined GBP1bn (pp.38-41). SEE uncertainties item 1: the GBP40m is not a comparable measure. (c) Betterment cycle (Tonon p.3): Development Charge 1947 abolished 1953; Betterment Levy 1967 repealed 1970; Development Land Tax 1976 removed 1985; Labour introduces, Conservatives repeal. Gibson 2025 Table 1.1 (printed p.10) confirms the dates (DC repealed from 18 Nov 1952 by the 1953 Act; levy ceased 22 Jul 1970, formal repeal 1971; DLT repealed 19 Mar 1985) but also lists a fourth tax, the Development Gains Tax (Conservative-proposed, 1973-76), which the essay omits. Essay adds Christophers (2018): about 10% of Britain's landmass moved from public to private ownership since 1979 (not verified; book not fetched) and Catney & Henneberry (2019): the post-1979 shift from state entitlement to negotiated contribution was a deliberate political choice (not read). (d) Scale claim (Tonon p.2): s106 and CIL deliver about 40% of England's affordable housing against about 20% from direct subsidy (Oxley 2008; Whitehead 2007), stated as 'today'. These are 2007-08 sources; do not repeat as current. BRAZIL, with the Tier 1 figures: (e) OODC formula (Tonon p.5): formula with a planning factor varying by location and a social-interest factor fully exempting social housing. Sandroni 2011 (Land Lines, July 2011): charge applies to the gap between maximum and basic floor-area ratio (basic FAR 1-2, maximum 1, 2, 2.5 or 4 by area, from the 2002 Strategic Master Plan and 2004 Land Use Law 13,885); planning factor discourages or encourages density by infrastructure and transit and differs for residential/non-residential use; social-interest coefficient runs 0 to 1 and is 0 for affordable housing and nonprofit hospitals, schools, cultural and religious uses; OODC receipts reached R$650m (about US$325m) in roughly five years, deposited in FUNDURB; revenue 'will fade' as buildable stock is exhausted, unlike recurring property tax. Friendly 2017 (printed p.17): OODC collected almost R$1.9bn 2004-2015 (about CAD$712m), average about R$145m a year, peak R$339.9m in 2011, roughly 1% of the city's gross revenue; collection concentrated in the southwest/'southeast quadrant' of expensive districts (printed p.19); 2015 receipts nearly 20% below 2013; the 2014 master plan was expected to raise receipts to about R$480m a year. Friendly fn35 (printed p.18): until the Land Value Register was created in 2014 the reference values were generally low and outdated; the 2014 plan updated them toward market values. (Tonon p.3 'PGV maintained substantially below market prices' cites Friendly 2017, consistent.) (f) CEPAC auctions (Tonon p.6: 'over USD 3 billion since 2004', cited to Amigo 2007; 'capturing the 2,000% uplift in Faria Lima', cited to Peterson 2009): Peterson 2009 printed pp.76-77 supports Faria Lima land value rising from US$300/sqm to US$7,000/sqm (about 23-fold, i.e. about +2,200%, 'reportedly'), and as of 2005 about 42% of the 2.25m sqm additional floor-space stock sold for R$320m (US$190m), development rights sold at up to R$1,100/sqm. Sandroni 2011: more than US$1bn raised from the Faria Lima and Agua Espraiada operations combined, kept inside each operation rather than going to FUNDURB. Mahendra et al. 2020 (WRI, summary pp.2-3 and the OUCAE fiscal-impact section): Agua Espraiada (OUCAE) sold 3.4 million CEPACs 2004-2012 for BRL 2.9bn (US$806m at R$3.65/$; average CEPAC price BRL 305 in 2004 rising to BRL 1,271 in 2012); with the OUCAE fund's financial returns the total was BRL 3.9bn from 2004 to January 2019; OODC citywide recorded BRL 2.7bn over the same period. The essay's '>USD 3bn' is not supported by any of these and is cited to a 2007 article that cannot contain post-2007 totals. (g) FUNDURB (Tonon p.6): 'at least 30% of OODC revenues and 25% of Urban Operations funds' mandatorily allocated to social housing in ZEIS; parity council. Friendly 2017 (printed p.15 and p.23): the FUNDURB council has been evenly divided between public sector and civil society only since the 2014 master plan (before 2014: 25 members, 16 government, 9 civil society; the 2002 plan left civil-society representation to executive discretion); the council meets four times a year and is accountable to the municipal urban development council; the 2014 plan earmarked 30% of FUNDURB funds for social housing (preferably in ZEIS, mainly land acquisition) and 30% for mobility; actual 2013-2015 spending: 28% housing (nearly 40% in 2015), 23% drainage and sanitation, 21% transit/cycle/roads, 10% pedestrian, total over R$800m; FUNDURB resources were prioritised in the periphery (a 'Robin Hood' pattern, printed p.26). The '25% of Urban Operations funds' figure was not found in Friendly or Mahendra (WRI says OUCAE's own CEPAC earmark rose from 10% in 2004 to 30% in 2018). (h) Agua Espraiada segregation risk (Tonon p.5): BRL 3.9bn raised by 2019 but about 60% went to roads serving higher-income residents, not social housing; over 800 families from Jardim Edite cleared. Mahendra et al. 2020: Table 1 (US$ millions, 2004-Jan 2019): total US$1,021.4m of investment, of which road system 608.4 (59.6%), social housing 228.8 (22.4%), Metro Line 17 106.7 (10.4%), public space 9.0 (0.9%), administration 68.4 (6.7%); the paper's summary says only 33.7% went to services directly benefiting low-income families and that 59.6% went to roads; at least 8,000 families displaced by construction in the area (WRI p.16); 'Jardim Edite' does not appear in the WRI paper. So the '60%' is of spending (not of the BRL 3.9bn), and the essay's family count is a different, much smaller, unverified number. (i) Pro-cyclicality and concentration (Tonon p.4): CEPACs raise money only in the high-value southwest; the Jabaquara operation's auctions drew no bidders (Biderman 2021, not reached); OODC receipts fell by half after 2008 (Nobre 2017, not reached). Sandroni 2011 says revenues 'increased annually' since introduction in spite of the crisis; Friendly shows a 2011 peak. T1 should treat the 'fell by half' claim as unverified and in tension with both. Friendly does support geographic concentration. Other Tier 1 leads in the essay's reference list the wiki lacks: OECD/Lincoln Institute (2022) Global Compendium of Land Value Capture Policies (doi 10.1787/4f9559ee-en); Cho et al. 2022 'Land Value Capture Across the Globe', Cityscape 24(3); Smolka 2013 Lincoln Policy Focus Report (Latin America; Barra da Tijuca 1,900% 1972-75); Alterman 2012 Oxford Handbook chapter; Ingram & Hong (eds) 2007 and 2012 (the wiki already cites Walters 2012 from the latter).

uncertainties: 1) JLE '67-fold' comparison is a scope mismatch, and T1 should not repeat it as a measurement divergence. Mitchell & Vickers (2003) Table 1 (printed p.18, PDF p.23) gives GBP0.04bn for Canary Wharf, but that is the domestic house-price uplift at Canada Water used as a surrogate for Canary Wharf and North Greenwich; the authors write that these stations 'should not be bracketed together and produce dubious results' because they are 'mainly commercial areas', and their total of about GBP9bn 'assumes that all land was in private residential use' with commercial uplift not captured. JLL's GBP300m-GBP2.7bn is described by Peterson as the land-value impact in Canary Wharf (presumably including commercial); the JLL report itself was not read. Peterson (a World Bank book) reports the three numbers side by side without this caveat and the essay inherits it. Safe wording: three studies commissioned or published 1999-2005 reached incompatible conclusions, partly because they measured different things; cite Peterson for the existence of the spread and Mitchell & Vickers for the scope. 2) Mis-sourced Brazil figures in the essay: '>USD 3bn since 2004' and 'US$100 to US$4,000 per sqm 1980-2008' are both cited to Amigo 2007, a 2007 article that cannot report totals or a 2008 endpoint; 'BRL 3.9bn by 2019' is the OUCAE total including financial returns (CEPAC sales alone BRL 2.9bn); the '800 families, Jardim Edite' figure is not in the WRI paper (which says at least 8,000 families displaced). Use the WRI/Sandroni/Friendly numbers directly. Amigo 2007 could not be fetched, so the US$100-4,000 claim is unchecked. 3) FUNDURB parity is recent: even council composition dates from the 2014 master plan (Friendly p.15); the essay's present-tense description hides that earlier councils had 9 of 25 civil-society seats. The 30%/25% earmarks: Friendly gives 30% housing and 30% mobility of FUNDURB funds; the essay's 25%-of-Urban-Operations figure is unsourced. 4) Citations in the essay that could not be checked: McAllister 2017 p.124; Crook & Whitehead 2019 p.375 quotation ('a more fundamental shift in the political economy of land'); Christophers 2018 '10% of landmass' (the wiki holds Christophers' Rentier Capitalism, not The New Enclosure); Nobre 2017; Biderman 2021; Wolf-Powers 2024; Fainstein 2010. 5) The 40%/20% s106-versus-subsidy affordable-housing split rests on 2007-08 sources and is not current. 6) Date of the 1967 levy's end: Gibson distinguishes 22 July 1970 (levy ceased) from the 1971 formal repeal; the essay says 1970, the wiki says 1971; either is defensible if the distinction is stated. 7) PDF metadata lists the file author as 'Niloy Sikder' (a LibreOffice template artefact; no bearing on authorship, which the Zenodo record and the title page give as Tonon). Zenodo lists no affiliation; the Oxford MSc affiliation is from the PDF title page and ORCID education entry only. 8) Partisan framing: the essay's 'Labour introduces, Conservatives repeal' omits the Conservative-proposed Development Gains Tax (1973-76) that Labour's DLT replaced (Gibson Table 1.1); Crook & Whitehead and Catney & Henneberry may support a looser 'political economy' reading, but neither was read.

claim_grade: B for what the abstract says (peer-reviewed single-case qualitative study, abstract-level, not independently verified); anything beyond the abstract (case details, figures, generalisation) unknown. Tier: journal-level peer review gives the paper citable standing for what it itself finds, but the author is not an established name on the 4c rubric (a researcher at a provincial social-science academy with no checked publication record), and the paper is a one-case study, so it supports nothing as a general proposition; it must never be listed as support for a Georgist claim.
content_summary: From the publisher abstract (OpenAlex copy): the study is a longitudinal case of how a service-oriented multinational corporation (MNC) was attracted to a Chinese industrial park, using grounded theory and actor-network theory (ANT). Definition: 'reverse rent-seeking' is rent-seeking in which 'the enterprise [is] the rent-setter and the local government the rent-seeker' (abstract's own wording). It is argued to have 'significantly contributed to the failure of investment promotion and undermined sustainable local operations'. Mechanism (abstract): it arose from the interaction of (i) an asymmetric reciprocal exchange that required the local government to provide resources, concessions and management authority without equivalent MNC commitment, creating 'rent-seeking space'; (ii) a two-sided principal-agent structure; (iii) information asymmetry; (iv) interest misalignment; the MNC's regional managers are the 'focal actors' who exploited the space through opportunism. Practical implications (abstract): standardise investment-promotion procedures and contractual documentation (contributions, ownership and treatment of assets and equipment specified); involve independent third-party oversight during negotiation and implementation; establish expert evaluation, disclosure and post-establishment monitoring. What is NOT in the abstract: the park, MNC, years, the value of concessions, any quantitative result. Reference list (84 deposited references, Crossref): classics Tullock 1980 ('Efficient Rent Seeking'), Krueger 1974, Murphy, Shleifer & Vishny 1993, Buchanan, Tollison & Tullock (eds) 1980, plus many Chinese-language works on development-zone management, government-business relations ('collusion' vs 'cooperation'), investment-promotion policy and local officials' promotion tournaments (Zhou Li-An 2007), and an ANT/grounded-theory methods literature. Titles only; no land-rent or Georgist literature appears among the titles. Georgist relevance, honestly: low. The concession of 'resources' to an investor is a form of public giveaway and the paper's remedies are transparency and contract discipline, which a Georgist can read as an illustration that discretionary, negotiated transfers of public assets create rent-seeking space (the same structural point as negotiated s106 viability, Carter's dual regulation on the existing page). But the abstract reports opportunism by an MNC's regional managers inside a principal-agent problem, not a general result on subsidy competition, and the 'rent' is concessions to one firm rather than land or resource rent.

content_summary: From the abstract (Crossref and OpenAlex agree): the paper says that, despite wide use of the term since Krueger (1974) and Tullock (1967), there is 'no unified consensus on its definition', particularly when transfers occur across time with sequential decision-making. It proposes a 'comprehensive, non-formalist framework' classifying rent transfers by the intertemporal sequencing of decisions, with a typology of five categories: Direct Resource Receipt (DRR), Direct Resource Extraction (DRE), Temporary Agreements (T), Transfer Reversal Negotiations (TRN) and Transfer Reversals (TR). It contrasts itself with 'the dominant mathematical contest-function models' and says it preserves the 'chronological messiness, provisionality, and institutional ambiguity' of real rent transfers, modelling rent-seeking as a 'sequenced process rather than a static equilibrium' and offering 'practical tools for empirical identification'. Not obtainable: any definitions of the five categories, examples, cases, data, or references. No claim about land, economic rent in the Ricardian sense, or Georgist policy appears in the abstract. Relation to existing material: it positions itself against the Tullock/Krueger/contest-function tradition (Tullock 1980 'Efficient Rent Seeking' and its successors) rather than adding to the Tullock-Krueger-Khan material on the wiki; nothing in the abstract engages Khan's distinction between damaging and growth-enhancing rents, which the page already carries.
